title: Class 11 Chemistry — Metals and Metallurgy Study Guide
notes: Metallurgy is extracting metals from ores and refining them. Hydrometallurgy uses aqueous solutions, pyrometallurgy uses high temperature, and electrometallurgy uses electrical energy. Gangue or matrix is unwanted ore material; flux reacts with gangue to form slag. An alloy is a metallic mixture; an amalgam contains mercury.

A typical extraction route includes concentration, conversion to a suitable compound, reduction and refining. Calcination heats an ore with limited/no air, often decomposing carbonates or hydroxides. Roasting usually heats sulfide ores in excess air, often forming oxides and SO₂. Smelting uses heat, reductant and flux to form molten metal and slag. Carbon reduction suits some oxides; thermite uses a more reactive metal such as aluminium; electrochemical reduction is used for highly reactive metals.

Poling uses reducing gases from green wood to remove oxide impurities from suitable molten metals. Electrorefining uses an impure anode, pure-metal cathode and electrolyte containing metal ions: target metal dissolves at the anode and deposits at the cathode; less reactive impurities may form anode mud.

Group 1 alkali metals have one valence electron, commonly form +1 ions, and become more reactive down the group. Sodium is extracted by electrolysis of molten NaCl in a Downs cell; CaCl₂ lowers the melting point. Sodium reacts vigorously with water to form NaOH and H₂. NaOH neutralizes acids and precipitates many metal hydroxides. Na₂CO₃ is an alkaline salt that releases CO₂ with acids.

Group 2 alkaline-earth metals commonly form +2 ions. Hydroxide solubility generally increases down the group, while sulfate solubility generally decreases; qualitative trends reflect lattice and hydration effects. Carbonate and nitrate thermal stability generally increases down the group as larger cations polarize the anion less. Common compounds: quicklime CaO; bleaching powder conventionally CaOCl₂; magnesia MgO; plaster of Paris CaSO₄·½H₂O; Epsom salt MgSO₄·7H₂O.
keyPoints: Select extraction methods according to ore composition and metal reactivity.
Calcination uses limited/no air; roasting is usually in excess air, especially for sulfides.
Flux plus gangue forms slag; roasting sulfides may release SO₂.
Downs process electrolyzes molten NaCl, not aqueous brine.
Group 2 hydroxide solubility generally rises down the group while sulfate solubility falls.
Memorize formulae and waters of crystallization for named industrial compounds.
practiceQuestions: Distinguish calcination from roasting and state which is used commonly for sulfide ores.
Explain the roles of flux and slag during smelting.
Describe Downs-cell products and why molten salt is used instead of aqueous NaCl.
Write formulae of plaster of Paris and Epsom salt, including waters of crystallization.
State general Group 2 down-group solubility trends for hydroxides and sulfates.
summary: Extraction choices follow ore type and metal reactivity. Know the metallurgical sequence and vocabulary, then connect periodic trends to sodium chemistry and common industrial salts.
